enhanced.fullText:
The Fraud Enforcement and Recovery Act of 2009 (FERA), codified at 31 U.S.C. § 3729-3733, significantly strengthened the False Claims Act (FCA) by expanding liability for fraudulent claims involving federal funds. For higher education institutions, FERA creates comprehensive obligations regarding the accurate use and reporting of federal grants, contracts, and financial aid programs.

FERA clarifies that liability under 31 U.S.C. § 3729(a)(1)(A) extends to any false or fraudulent claim for government money or property, regardless of whether the claim is presented directly to a government official, whether the government has physical custody of funds, or whether the defendant specifically intended to defraud the government. This expansion is particularly significant for universities receiving federal research grants, Title IV financial aid, and other federal funding streams.

Key provisions under 31 U.S.C. § 3729(a)(1)(B) expand liability to sub-recipients of federal funds, meaning that universities must ensure compliance not only in their direct federal dealings but also in their oversight of subcontractors, research partners, and third-party service providers. Universities receiving federal funds through programs administered under 20 U.S.C. Chapter 28 (Higher Education Act) and 42 U.S.C. Chapter 16 (National Science Foundation) face enhanced scrutiny.

FERA reduces the knowledge standard from "specific intent" to "knowing" conduct, defined under 31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)(A) as actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance, or reckless disregard of truth or falsity. Universities must implement robust internal controls to prevent inadvertent violations in grant reporting, student enrollment certifications, and research expenditure documentation.

Enforcement mechanisms include civil penalties of $11,803 to $23,607 per false claim (adjusted annually under 28 CFR § 85.5), plus treble damages. The Department of Justice and various agency Inspectors General actively pursue FERA violations in higher education, particularly involving research misconduct, improper cost transfers, and financial aid fraud.

Whistleblower protections under 31 U.S.C. § 3730(h) encourage reporting of violations, with qui tam relators eligible for 15-30% of recovered funds. Universities must establish anti-retaliation policies and internal reporting mechanisms to address potential violations before they escalate to federal enforcement actions.

Recent enforcement trends focus on cybersecurity grant compliance, COVID-19 relief fund usage, and research integrity violations, requiring universities to maintain comprehensive documentation and implement regular compliance auditing procedures.
enhanced.summary: FERA expands False Claims Act liability to cover any fraudulent claim for federal funds, including sub-recipients. Universities must ensure accurate reporting and use of all federal grants, financial aid, and contracts, with civil penalties up to $23,607 per violation plus treble damages.
enhanced.requirements:
## Core Compliance Obligations
- Implement robust internal controls for all federal fund usage and reporting under 31 U.S.C. § 3729
- Establish comprehensive oversight of subcontractors and research partners receiving federal sub-awards
- Maintain accurate documentation for grant expenditures, student enrollment certifications, and research activities
- Train personnel on "knowing" conduct standards and fraud prevention

## Sub-recipient Monitoring
- Conduct due diligence on all entities receiving federal sub-awards
- Implement ongoing monitoring procedures for sub-recipient compliance
- Establish contractual compliance requirements in all sub-award agreements

## Internal Controls and Reporting
- Develop anti-retaliation policies protecting whistleblowers under 31 U.S.C. § 3730(h)
- Create internal reporting mechanisms for potential FERA violations
- Conduct regular compliance audits of federal funding programs
- Implement segregation of duties in grant administration and financial reporting processes
enhanced.reportingRequirements: No specific periodic reporting requirements under FERA itself. Universities must maintain accurate records for all federal grant reports, financial aid certifications, and compliance documentation as required by underlying federal programs. Suspected violations must be reported to appropriate federal agencies immediately upon discovery.
